light: Monstera deliciosa grows under the canopy in Central American rainforests, climbing tree trunks toward gaps in the leaves above. That habit explains what it wants indoors: bright, filtered light rather than bare sun. An east window, or a spot two to three feet back from a south or west window, is close to ideal.

Light is also what controls fenestration — the famous holes and splits. Juvenile leaves are solid hearts, and the plant only starts producing split leaves once it has enough light and maturity to support them. A Monstera in a dim corner will stay alive for years and never fenestrate. If yours is pushing out small, solid leaves, low light is the first thing to correct.
water: Water when the top two inches of mix have dried out. In a bright spot through spring and summer that usually lands somewhere around every seven to ten days, but treat that as a starting point rather than a schedule — pot size, mix and light all move the number. Water thoroughly until it runs from the drainage holes, then empty the saucer.

From late autumn through winter, growth slows and the mix stays wet far longer. Stretch the interval to every two or three weeks and check with a finger each time rather than watering on autopilot. More Monsteras are killed by winter watering habits carried over from summer than by any pest.

Monstera tolerates average household humidity, but it grows faster and produces better leaves above 60%. Grouping plants, a pebble tray or a humidifier all help. Misting looks appealing but raises humidity for only a few minutes.
soil: Use a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix rather than straight potting soil. A reliable blend is roughly one third quality potting mix, one third orchid bark and one third perlite, with a couple of handfuls of coco coir or worm castings for moisture retention and nutrition. The bark keeps air pockets around the roots, which is exactly what an epiphytic climber expects.

Whatever you mix, the pot must have drainage holes. Monstera roots rot quickly in a sealed cachepot that collects water at the bottom. Feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser at half strength every four weeks during spring and summer, and stop entirely over winter.

propagation: Monstera propagates readily from stem cuttings, and the single thing that determines success is whether your cutting includes a node. The node is the slightly raised band on the stem where a leaf meets it, often with a brown aerial root emerging. A leaf with no node will sit in water looking healthy for months and never root, because all the growth tissue is in the node.

Cut just below a node with clean shears, taking one or two leaves with it. Put the cutting in water, keeping the node submerged and the leaves out, in bright indirect light. Change the water weekly. Roots usually appear within two to four weeks; once several are two to three inches long, pot into your usual aroid mix and keep it slightly moister than normal for the first fortnight while the plant transitions from water roots to soil roots. You can also root cuttings directly in damp sphagnum moss, which skips that transition entirely and tends to produce sturdier plants.

problems.symptom: New leaves have no splits or holes
problems.cause: Not enough light, or a plant that is simply still young. Fenestration develops with maturity and adequate light, and it will not appear on a plant kept in a dim corner.
problems.fix: Move it closer to a bright window with filtered light and give it something to climb — a moss pole encourages the plant to produce larger, more mature leaves. Expect the change to show on new growth, not on existing leaves.

problems.symptom: Yellowing lower leaves
problems.cause: Most often overwatering, especially if several leaves yellow at once and the mix is still damp days after watering. A single old leaf yellowing near the base is just normal ageing.
problems.fix: Check the mix before every watering and let the top two inches dry out. If the soil smells sour or the roots are brown and soft, repot into fresh, chunky mix and trim the damaged roots.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Low humidity, underwatering, or salt buildup from fertiliser and hard tap water.
problems.fix: Raise humidity, water more consistently, and flush the pot thoroughly with plain water every few months to wash out accumulated salts.

problems.symptom: Dark brown patches with yellow halos
problems.cause: Bacterial or fungal leaf spot, usually following water sitting on the foliage in a cool, still room.
problems.fix: Remove affected leaves, improve air circulation, and water the soil rather than the leaves. Avoid misting until it clears.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing and stippled, dull leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor air and are easy to miss until the webbing appears.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant in the shower, then treat every five to seven days with insecticidal soap or neem oil for at least three cycles to catch newly hatched mites. Raising humidity makes reinfestation less likely.

problems.symptom: White cottony clusters in leaf joints
problems.cause: Mealybugs, which shelter where the leaf stem meets the main stem and in the folds of new growth.
problems.fix: Dab each cluster with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol, then follow with insecticidal soap. Check weekly for a month — they hide well and one missed cluster restarts the infestation.

problems.symptom: Stems growing long and leggy with small leaves
problems.cause: Insufficient light, and often a lack of support. Monstera is a climber, and an unsupported plant sprawls rather than building size.
problems.fix: Increase light and add a moss pole or trellis, tying the stem in so aerial roots can grip. Prune leggy sections back to a node and propagate the cuttings.

repotting: Repot every two to three years, or when roots grow out of the drainage holes, water runs straight through without wetting the mix, or the plant dries out far faster than it used to. Spring and early summer are the best time, so the plant recovers during active growth.

Go up only one pot size — roughly two inches wider in diameter. An oversized pot holds more wet mix than the roots can use, which is a common route to root rot. Slide the plant out, loosen the outer roots, cut away anything brown and mushy, and settle it into fresh aroid mix at the same depth it was growing before.

This is also the natural moment to add or replace a moss pole, since you can position it against the stem while the root ball is out of the pot. Water thoroughly after repotting, then hold off on fertiliser for four to six weeks while the roots settle.
varieties: The plain species is the most common, but several forms are worth knowing. 'Thai Constellation' carries creamy, speckled variegation, is tissue-cultured, and is more stable and more widely available than it once was. The 'Albo Variegata' form produces dramatic blocks of pure white, propagates only by cutting, and is far more temperamental — a cutting with too much white lacks the chlorophyll to sustain itself.

Do not confuse Monstera deliciosa with Monstera adansonii, sold as the Swiss cheese vine, which has smaller leaves with enclosed holes rather than splits that reach the edge. Young deliciosa plants are also frequently mislabelled as split-leaf philodendron, a different genus entirely. 'Borsigiana' is a faster, more compact growth form of deliciosa rather than a separate species.

light: Snake plant has a reputation as a low-light plant, and it is genuinely one of the most shade-tolerant houseplants available — but tolerating and thriving are different things. In a dark corner it survives almost indefinitely while putting out very little new growth. In bright indirect light it grows noticeably faster and keeps its variegation sharp.

It also handles a few hours of direct sun better than most houseplants, provided the change is gradual. Moving one straight from a shaded corner to a sunny south window will bleach or scorch the leaves, so shift it in stages over two or three weeks.
water: This is a succulent, and it stores water in its leaves. Water deeply, then let the mix dry out completely before watering again. Through spring and summer that is typically every two to three weeks; check by pushing a finger a couple of inches into the mix rather than watering on a schedule.

In winter, growth effectively stops and the plant needs remarkably little — once every four to six weeks is often plenty, and in a cool room it can go longer. Overwatering in winter is by far the most common way snake plants are killed.
Always water into the mix rather than down into the central rosette, where trapped water causes the base of the leaves to rot. Humidity is irrelevant to this plant; average household air is fine.
soil: Use a free-draining cactus or succulent mix, or make your own with two parts potting mix to one part coarse sand or perlite. The aim is a medium that wets through and then dries quickly rather than staying damp.

Terracotta suits snake plants particularly well because the porous walls pull moisture out of the mix between waterings. Drainage holes are essential. Feed lightly — a balanced fertiliser at half strength two or three times across the whole growing season is ample, and none at all through winter.

propagation: Division is the fastest and most reliable method, and it is the only one that preserves variegation. Slide the plant out of its pot and look for natural clumps with their own roots and rhizome; separate them with a clean knife, leaving each division at least three leaves and a healthy piece of rhizome. Pot each into dry cactus mix and wait a week before the first watering so cut surfaces can callus.

Leaf cuttings also work, with one important caveat: cuttings taken from a variegated plant such as 'Laurentii' will root and grow, but they revert to plain green, because the yellow margin is not carried in the leaf tissue. Cut a healthy leaf into three-inch sections, keeping track of which end pointed down — a section planted upside down will never root. Let the pieces callus for a day or two, then stand them bottom-end down in barely moist mix. Roots take a month or more, and a new pup several months after that. Patience is the main requirement.

problems.symptom: Leaves soft and mushy at the base
problems.cause: Root or rhizome rot from overwatering, a mix that holds too much moisture, or water sitting in the central rosette.
problems.fix: Unpot immediately, cut away every soft root and rhizome section until only firm white tissue remains, let the cuts dry for a day, and repot into dry cactus mix. Wait a week before watering. If the rot has reached most of the rhizome, save healthy leaves as cuttings instead.

problems.symptom: Leaves wrinkled, curling inward or creased lengthwise
problems.cause: Underwatering. A snake plant draws down its own water reserves before showing any distress, so wrinkling means it has been dry for a while.
problems.fix: Water thoroughly until it drains, and check again in a week. The leaves plump back up over several days. If it has been bone dry for months, water twice a week apart rather than trying to correct it in one go.

problems.symptom: Yellowing along the leaf margins
problems.cause: Usually overwatering, occasionally a pot-bound plant that can no longer take up water evenly.
problems.fix: Let the mix dry out completely and extend the interval. If the roots have filled the pot and are circling tightly, repot in spring.

problems.symptom: Brown, dry leaf tips
problems.cause: Inconsistent watering — long droughts followed by a soaking — or fluoride and salts in tap water.
problems.fix: Water more evenly, and try filtered or rainwater if your supply is hard. Trim the brown tip at an angle with clean scissors; it will not turn green again but it will stop advancing.

problems.symptom: Leaves falling over away from the centre
problems.cause: Most often too little light, causing weak growth that cannot hold itself up. Overwatering and a pot too large for the root mass also cause it.
problems.fix: Move to brighter light and reduce watering. A pot that is snug rather than roomy helps keep tall leaves upright; snake plants genuinely prefer being a little pot-bound.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps on leaves that scrape off
problems.cause: Scale insects, which attach themselves and feed under a hard protective shell.
problems.fix: Scrape them off with a fingernail or a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol, then treat with neem oil. Repeat every week for a month, since the mobile juveniles are almost invisible.

problems.symptom: Variegated leaves reverting to plain green
problems.cause: Insufficient light, or growth that originated from a leaf cutting rather than division.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light. Remove fully green new shoots if you want to keep the variegated look, and propagate variegated plants by division rather than leaf cuttings.

repotting: Snake plants are happy tight in their pots and only need repotting every three to five years. The usual prompt is dramatic: the rhizomes are strong enough to crack a plastic pot or push the whole plant upward out of the soil.

Repot in spring into a container just one size larger. Choose something heavy and wide rather than tall — mature leaves are top-heavy, and a light plastic pot tips over. Terracotta is ideal for both weight and moisture control.
Use the opportunity to divide crowded clumps and inspect the rhizome for soft spots. Pot at the same depth, water lightly after a week, and skip fertiliser for a couple of months.
varieties: Sansevieria trifasciata 'Laurentii' is the classic, with bold yellow margins on dark green. 'Zeylanica' has wavy silver-green banding and no yellow edge. 'Moonshine' is a pale silvery-green throughout and needs decent light to hold that colour.

For smaller spaces, 'Hahnii' — the bird's nest snake plant — forms a squat rosette six to eight inches tall. At the other extreme, Sansevieria masoniana, the whale fin, produces a single enormous paddle-shaped leaf. Note that the genus was reclassified into Dracaena, so you may see these sold as Dracaena trifasciata; the care is identical whichever name is on the label.

light: Golden pothos is genuinely adaptable, which is why it turns up in offices and windowless bathrooms. It grows in anything from low light to bright indirect light. What changes with light levels is not survival but appearance: in bright indirect light the leaves are larger and the golden variegation is pronounced, while in low light new leaves come out smaller and mostly green.
Avoid direct midday sun, which scorches the foliage and bleaches the variegation to a washed-out cream. If your plant is losing its gold, move it brighter before assuming it is a watering problem.
water: Let the top one to two inches of mix dry before watering, then water thoroughly until it drains. In a moderately bright spot during spring and summer this tends to be every seven to ten days, less in lower light where the mix stays damp longer.
Reduce through autumn and winter, often to every two to three weeks. Pothos is forgiving of a missed watering and distinctly unforgiving of a permanently wet pot, so when in doubt, wait.

The plant gives clear signals: leaves go slightly limp and soft when thirsty and perk up within hours of watering. Use that as your guide rather than a fixed schedule, but do not let wilting become routine — repeated severe drought causes permanent leaf loss along the vine.
soil: An ordinary well-draining houseplant mix works. Adding a handful of perlite or orchid bark improves aeration and makes overwatering harder to achieve, which is worth doing if you tend to water generously.

Pothos also grows indefinitely in plain water, which is why cuttings in jars do so well. A plant grown permanently in water needs a weak dose of liquid fertiliser every month or so, since there are no nutrients in the water itself. In soil, feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer only.

propagation: Pothos is one of the easiest houseplants to propagate, and it is a good first attempt if you have never taken a cutting. Find a node — the small brown nub on the vine where a leaf stem joins, often with a stubby aerial root already showing — and cut half an inch below it. Each cutting needs at least one node and one leaf.

Stand the cuttings in a glass of water with the nodes submerged and the leaves above the surface, in bright indirect light. Change the water weekly to keep it oxygenated. Roots normally appear within one to two weeks, and once they reach two to three inches you can pot several cuttings together into one pot for a full-looking plant straight away. Keep newly potted cuttings a little moister than an established plant for the first couple of weeks. Cuttings can equally be pushed straight into damp soil, skipping water entirely; the rooting is slower to watch but the plant adapts faster.

problems.symptom: Yellow leaves, often several at once
problems.cause: Overwatering is the usual cause, particularly if the mix is still wet and the yellowing starts at the base of the plant.
problems.fix: Let the top inches dry properly before the next watering and empty any water standing in the cachepot. One yellow leaf occasionally is normal ageing and not a concern.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf tips and edges
problems.cause: Dry air, underwatering, or accumulated fertiliser salts and chlorine from tap water.
problems.fix: Water more consistently, flush the pot with plain water every few months, and consider filtered water if your tap water is heavily treated.

problems.symptom: Long bare vines with widely spaced leaves
problems.cause: Too little light. The plant stretches toward the nearest source, producing distance between leaves rather than new foliage.
problems.fix: Move it brighter and prune the bare vines back to within a few inches of the soil. Pothos branches readily from pruned nodes, and the cuttings you removed can be rooted and added back to the same pot.

problems.symptom: Variegation fading to plain green
problems.cause: Insufficient light. The gold-marked tissue contains less chlorophyll, so in dim conditions the plant favours green growth.
problems.fix: Increase light gradually. Cut back fully green vines to encourage variegated growth from lower nodes.

problems.symptom: Black or dark brown stem bases, plant collapsing
problems.cause: Root rot from prolonged wet soil, sometimes with a sour smell from the mix.
problems.fix: Take healthy cuttings from the upper vines immediately as insurance, then unpot, trim all soft black roots, and repot into fresh mix in a pot with drainage. Water sparingly until new growth appears.

problems.symptom: Small flies rising from the soil
problems.cause: Fungus gnats, which breed in permanently damp topsoil and are a symptom of watering too often.
problems.fix: Let the top layer dry fully between waterings, use yellow sticky traps for the adults, and water from below for a few weeks. The problem resolves once the surface stops staying wet.

problems.symptom: Leaves limp and drooping despite damp soil
problems.cause: Root rot rather than thirst. Damaged roots cannot take up water, so the plant wilts even in wet mix.
problems.fix: Check the roots. Healthy roots are firm and white; rotted ones are brown and fall apart. Trim, repot into fresh mix, and reduce watering frequency.

repotting: Pothos grows fast and generally needs a new pot every one to two years. Signs are roots emerging from the drainage holes, water running straight through, or growth slowing noticeably during the growing season.

Move up one size, about two inches wider. Spring is best but pothos is tolerant enough to repot at almost any time. Tease apart circling roots at the base of the root ball so they grow outward rather than continuing to spiral.

If the plant has gone bare and leggy at the top, repotting is a good moment to cut it back hard and replant rooted cuttings around the parent to thicken it up. Water well afterwards and wait a month before resuming fertiliser.
varieties: 'Golden' is the familiar green-and-yellow form. 'Marble Queen' is heavily streaked with white and grows more slowly, since it carries less chlorophyll. 'Neon' is a uniform chartreuse with no variegation at all and keeps its colour best in bright indirect light.

'N'Joy' and 'Pearls and Jade' are compact, with distinct white-bordered leaves. 'Satin pothos' is sold alongside these but is actually Scindapsus pictus, a different genus with velvety, silver-spotted leaves — care is very similar. Note that all pothos varieties are toxic to cats and dogs if chewed, so a hanging position is worth considering in a pet household.
